If you're making software that is designed to parse complex, diverse data, especially when YOU don't control the data, and it is generated in varied ways by thousands of different organizations or users, then there's really no substitute for what's known as "fuzzing" tests.

Fuzzing is a testing technique where you try to intelligently generate a huge number of varied inputs to your program, with the goal of finding parsing bugs that you'd be unlikely to come across if you're only testing with a fixed set of valid inputs.

A naive approach to generating random inputs would be wasteful, since most inputs are trivially invalid and can be quickly rejected.

What you really want are inputs that are pathological; ones that are nearly valid but have some bizarre issue that can confuse your parsing rules and trigger code pathways that you'd normally never traverse.

Fuzzing used to be a somewhat esoteric approach used by security-focused engineers in high-stakes, sophisticated applications. But now anyone can use it. I have a skill specifically for fuzzing you can try here:

https://t.co/4GXFLCYvWD

It's part of a series of testing-related skills that also includes metamorphic testing, conformance harness testing, golden artifact generation, end-to-end integration testing, etc. 

The skill works across many popular languages and automatically installs the needed tooling for you, instruments your application for fuzzing, and then mounts extended fuzz testing campaigns. 

You can see an example of one in the screenshot, where it's been working for many hours, subjecting three different parsers in my hedge_fund_data_tool to torture tests. 

For instance, my elaborate parser for SEC insider trade forms (i.e., Forms 3, 4, and 5), which is thousands of lines of Rust, has been called over 780 million times, each invocation with a different, optimally selected input designed to best explore all the different possible code paths within the parser.

There aren't that many forms of this kind in the history of the SEC's EDGAR database, across all companies. The only way to do something like that is with fuzzing. And now you can!

More and more, I’m realizing that the use of external library dependencies in Rust projects is an anti-pattern. 

Most libraries are one-size-fits-all, with scope creep and sprawling dependency chains that lead to you depending on hundreds of different projects and people, any one of which could suffer from a supply-chain attack.

They also often rely on C or C++ libraries, which defeats the benefit of the strict memory safety that is the major selling point of Rust. This usually results in complex and annoying build processes that create headaches when you want everything to be cross-platform.

And even when they don’t use C or C++ libraries, they almost always make liberal use of unsafe code. If you don’t make strict memory safety a basic requirement, it’s easy to slip into bad patterns out of convenience or a sense of misguided pragmatism.

Perhaps worst of all, they are just not performance-optimized the way things can and should be today, with special tricks to optimize performance specifically on Apple silicon or on high-core-count AMD processors. 

Those two platforms have very different performance characteristics and need specialized designs to even approach the point of saturating the hardware.

For my FrankenSearch project, which is the core of my cass tool and also used in various other projects of mine like agent mail and eidetic engine, I have been using the Tantivy library for fast lexical search. 

Tantivy is sort of a Rust descendant of Lucene, which is the core search system used in Elasticsearch. 

I realized recently that many of the things that annoy me about FrankenSearch come from Tantivy, and I hate the feeling that it’s a walled-off dependency that I don’t want to change for the obvious reasons. 

Since for my newest projects (e.g., FrankenOCR, FrankenMarkdown, FrankenSim, and FrankenGraphDB), I have a strict “no outside dependencies” rule other than my own projects like Asupersync and FrankenSQLite, I decided that I should start applying a similar standard in my older projects. 

That’s why I decided to create my own specialized lexical search system optimized specifically for FrankenSearch. I’ve made the plan for it and the implementation work is already far along. You can see the plan here:

https://t.co/8PHIpapyOU

This will reduce the number of dependencies by 41 crates, increase safety and security, and dramatically increase performance. 

And because this module will be part of the core code of the system, it will benefit along with the rest of the projects from my endless continuous performance optimization campaigns, so it will keep getting faster and faster.

As the plan explains, the biggest wins come from not paying the “generality tax.” By not trying to be all things to all people, we can do just what we need in the absolute optimal way possible.

BOOM! Well, I'll be damned if that's not the very BEST-sounding, 100% simulated/synthesized concert grand piano I've ever heard!

https://t.co/iu5sbvEJ6I

What does that mean? ZERO recordings of real-world sounds were used (other than for comparison and diagnosis), nor were any measurements captured by microphones or similar.

Literally everything from start to finish here was part of an enormously intricate physics simulation of a piano: its geometry, materials, moving parts, and acoustic radiation.

Oh, and I did the same thing for a full drum kit and cymbals. The cymbals are modelled using the estimated geometry and dimpling pattern of a real Zildjian splash cymbal, together with estimated profile details and literature-based properties for B20 bronze alloy.

For the most extreme audio quality, you can pre-render to WAV files or similar. But after many, many rounds of iterative performance optimization, I now have the wasm version running at better than real-time, so it sounds really good live in the browser as well!

This is a big deal. It's shockingly hard to get truly realistic-sounding audio from synthesized instruments. The real world is just too complicated. What people usually end up doing is spending hundreds or thousands of dollars to buy these massive libraries of recorded sounds of a real piano, which takes up many gigs of space and is super slow to use.

The worst part of that approach isn't the size of the files, the cost of the sample packs, or the inelegance of the approach. It's that EVEN THAT is a massive simplification, because they are recording each key separately at various key velocities and so forth.

That means they are missing the very complex interaction effects that arise in a real piano when you play certain keys at the same time or after one another. The energy persists in the instrument and conditions the next sounds.

It's subtle but real and you pick up on it when it's missing. And yes, they do try to capture some of this, but they use very lossy methods with more simplified approximations that are way more primitive than what I'm doing here with FrankenSim.

I've invested a massive amount of time and focus on ensuring that the energy accounting is correct in these simulations.

And the same thing goes for drums! There are complex interaction effects. These sorts of things are emergent and "just fall out" when everything is simulated for REAL using the actual underlying physics.

So why haven't other companies and people done this? I'm not actually sure; it's kind of insane when you consider all those people working at Yamaha, Roland, Korg, Moog, etc. But my guess is that it's because it's super hard and complicated to get all the physics right and to program it the right way so that it's tractable without needing crazy amounts of compute.

Anyway, take a look at this demo site I set up. It's a lot of fun to play with, and at the bottom there is a nifty MIDI player that takes any MIDI file and lets you listen to it with the high-quality simulated piano and drums in the browser.

This is the culmination of months of work and hundreds of billions of frontier tokens. It all started when I wanted to see what Fable 5 could really do, so I thought of the most comically ambitious project I could think of: FrankenSim, the system that unifies ALL of physics into a single coherent and cohesive simulation across all domains: mechanics, fluid dynamics, electricity and magnetism, etc., instead of modeling each domain as a separate silo, where each domain can use the same generic geometric primitives, solvers, calculus machinery, etc.

All unified using the language of sheaf cohomology to maintain consistency between representations, and where everything is made as legible, intuitive, and ergonomic to AI agents as possible.

This music simulation stuff is just the beginning. Beyond many more instruments, I'm going to be using FrankenSim to model HVAC systems, fluid flow through plumbing systems, and more!

Small RL companies are the AI industry's equivalent of quant shops. Let me explain.

Both are small, secretive, full of brilliant people, profitable, and always one step from their edge disappearing.

The parallels:

- Secretive. Nobody publishes their signals. Labs won't say what they're training next, and vendors can't say who they sell to. Epoch calls the market "largely behind closed doors."

- Hunting alpha. For a quant, a trade stops working once everyone finds it. For these shops, a task stops paying once models can solve it (labs drop tasks at around 70% pass rate). Meanwhile, labs are building their own in-house. So they always have to find the next field.

- Deep Industry Connections. You need to know the problem cold to get in. Founders have usually worked at, or sold to, the labs. You can't define "correct" for fund accounting without having done fund accounting.

- They buy strange data. Quants buy satellite photos of parking lots. RL shops bid for enterprise data (eg $12.5M bid for Spirit Airlines historical data).

- Brilliant people. Quants hire math olympiad winners. These shops hire ex-lab researchers and real practitioners.

- Huge revenue per head. Jane Street made about $11M per employee in 2025. Proximal is about $5M. The tweet's company would be $20M.

- One narrow problem that makes something more efficient. Quants make markets more efficient. These RL shops make models training more efficient.

- High risk (for different reasons). A quant can lose millions in a day on a bad trade. An RL shop's risk is that one lab trains a model that makes their environments irrelevant, or brings the work in-house, and the revenue stops.

- Overfitting/reward hacking. A quant's nightmare is a strategy that looks perfect on historical data and fails live. An RL shop's nightmare is an RL grader that scores perfectly and trains the model incorrectly. 

- Infrastructure arms race. Quants pay for microseconds of speed. RL shops race to spin up thousands of disposable computers per training run.

Obviously there are as many differences between RL companies and quant shops, but right now the aura around them feels eerily similar. 

Curious to see how this market matures as robotics opens up a new surface, and whether the frontier labs end up absorbing them.

TLDR Ultimately, housing prices reflect more than the cost of construction. They reflect land administration, infrastructure, economic concentration, supply constraints, and the availability of alternative investment assets.

Long version 
The cost of housing in Nigeria goes beyond design. I can't stand the soulless architecture of many so called luxury homes here, but I understand that a lot more goes into property pricing than the quality of the building itself.

Consider location, access to infrastructure, security, and proximity to business districts.

Few Nigerian cities have the economic pull of Lagos. Even within Lagos, the number of locations with decent infrastructure, security, and convenient access to business districts is limited relative to demand.

Then there's our suboptimal land administration system, where obtaining properly titled land can be an incredibly difficult process.

All of this is compounded by the limited investment options available to Nigerians. Housing isn't just accommodation; it's also an investment asset. Property prices are driven not only by the need for shelter but also by investors looking to preserve and grow their wealth.

These factors contribute to the insane property valuations we see in Nigeria's major cities.

This is why blindly comparing Nigerian property prices with those in South Africa or the US misses the bigger picture.

Yes, American homes are generally better built, with better infrastructure and more reliable public services. But the US also has a much larger number of locations with good infrastructure and economic opportunities, giving people more options and creating competition that helps moderate prices.

There's also a much deeper and more accessible investment market in the US. People can invest in the S&P 500, bonds, and other financial instruments instead of relying so heavily on real estate to preserve their wealth.

When people have more viable investment options, less capital is forced into property.

Ultimately, housing prices reflect more than the cost of construction. They reflect land administration, infrastructure, economic concentration, supply constraints, and the availability of alternative investment assets.

Until we address these underlying issues, comparing property prices across countries without considering their different economic realities will always be an incomplete argument.

there’s a particular kind of 30-year-old guy who is still psychologically living in the best year of his life.
he had something happen at 24.
a startup took off. a job paid absurdly well. an investment worked. someone important noticed him. for about eleven months, the future looked completely obvious.
he was going to be somebody.
then the thing stopped working.
six years later, he’s still negotiating with the version of himself who thought he had already figured life out.

i think early success can do something genuinely cruel to a person if it arrives before they’ve learned how to be ordinary.
it teaches you to associate your identity with acceleration.
you’re the promising one.
the guy who figured it out young.
the one relatives ask about at thanksgiving because apparently something exciting is always happening with you.
until it isn't.

now you're 31, your income is inconsistent, your friends are buying houses, and you're explaining another business idea to your parents over dinner.
your dad asks whether you've considered getting a regular job.
you hear it as a request to identify the exact moment your life went wrong.

the complicated part is that you probably could get a decent job.
you have a degree. you know how to speak professionally. you have contacts. you understand enough corporate language to survive a meeting about absolutely nothing.
but somewhere along the way, a normal salary became psychologically associated with surrender.

you spent so many years imagining yourself escaping the system that participating in it now feels humiliating.
meanwhile the person who accepted a boring job at 25 has been promoted twice, developed useful relationships, saved money, and learned how to operate inside an actual organization.
you have seventeen tabs open about starting an AI company.
one of them is a youtube video called "why 2026 will create more millionaires than ever."
it's 1:38 am.

this is the part i find genuinely sad.
sometimes family money gives people just enough protection from consequences to keep an identity crisis running for years.
there's no spectacular collapse.
just a long, quiet decline in options.
the ambition stays enormous while the evidence gets smaller.
you start avoiding old friends because their perfectly normal questions require increasingly elaborate answers.
"what are you working on these days?"
god.

you used to love that question.
eventually you become more committed to preserving the possibility of an extraordinary future than doing the fairly unimpressive things that might actually produce one.

and nobody wants to talk about how addictive potential can be.
potential is wonderful because it never has to submit quarterly results.
you can be brilliant in theory for decades.

you can keep insisting that you're one connection, one opportunity, one launch away.
the really painful possibility is that your first success was real, your ambition is real, and you still have to start again at the bottom of something.
at 31.

with people younger than you.
without making a speech about how you used to be ahead.
some guys would genuinely rather spend another five years being a future millionaire than spend six months being a beginner.
and the worst part is they know exactly what they're doing.

they just can't bear to have anyone watch them start over.
